newsitem.title: BRAZIL: U.N. sees cocaine routes changing in South America.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sees cocaine routes changing in South America.

text.p: The emergence of Peru and Bolivia as cocaine-producing nations to match Colombia will alter shipment routes of the drug through South America, a United Nations official said on Thursday.

Brazil, Argentina and Chile could see big increases in the amount of cocaine passing through their borders, and higher consumption, said Aldo Lale-Demoz, Latin America and Caribbean director of the U.N.'s International Drugs Control Programme.

"If Peru and Bolivia continue to grow as producers of cocaine...the logical route for this trade will be through Argentina, Chile and Brazil," he said at a news conference to present a U.N. world drugs report.

Colombia accounts for 60 percent of the roughly 850 tonnes of cocaine produced in the Andean region each year. Shipments tend to go north through the Caribbean or via Central America and Mexico to the United States, the world's biggest market.
Only two or three percent of Colombia's cocaine is thought to pass through Brazil, which is already struggling to stem that flow.

U.N. officials believe intense anti-drugs operations in Colombia are provoking a boom in refining of cocaine in Peru and Bolivia. For years they have produced large amounts of coca leaf and paste which is sent to Colombia to be turned into cocaine.
Now drug gangs are setting up labs in Peru and Bolivia and much of the cocaine they produce would probably head south before being shipped to the United States, Lale-Demoz said.
The diversification of cocaine refining across the Andean region would also make it harder for law enforcement officials to trace the reverse trade in chemicals needed to produce the drug, he said.
"It is very important that training and policies are carried out on a regional level because this problem has a regional dimension," he said.
Already much of the cocaine seized in the drug-riven shanty-towns of Rio de Janeiro comes from Bolivia, said Luis Matias Flach, president of Brazil's Federal Drugs Council.

Lale-Demoz also urged Brazil to take steps to fight an expected surge in consumption of amphetamines and ecstasy which is on the rise in other parts of the world but remains relatively rare in South America.

"Brazil has everything needed to produce the new types of chemical drugs. We must be worried about tomorrow. It is quite probable these new drugs will be challenging the Brazilian authorities soon," he said.
